analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime for companies to delay reporting serious product dangers to regulators, workers, or the public.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced in July 2014 and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, it died there when the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime, punishable by up to five years in prison, for a company or its responsible executives to sit on knowledge of a serious danger from a product, service, or business practice. Within 24 hours of learning of such a danger they would have to tell a federal agency by phone, within 15 days in writing, and warn exposed workers and other identifiable people as soon as possible. It would also make it illegal to fire or punish an employee for making such a report, with court enforcement, and would bar companies from paying an executive's fine out of corporate funds. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and consumers exposed to dangerous products and practices, because companies and their executives would face prison time for concealing known dangers, and employees who speak up would get new legal protection against being fired. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and consumers near hidden dangers

how_it_helps.text: Companies and responsible executives must verbally report a serious danger to a federal agency within 24 hours, in writing within 15 days, and warn affected workers and identifiable exposed individuals as soon as practicable. [S2] [S3]
Knowing failure to do so carries a fine, up to five years in prison, or both, and an individual's fine cannot be paid out of company assets. [S3]

Retaliating against an employee who reports a danger or warns others would be unlawful, with remedies including reinstatement, back pay, attorney fees, and a right to a jury trial; mandatory arbitration of these claims would not be enforceable. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Companies that make or sell products and services in interstate commerce, and the individual executives responsible for reporting, who would face new criminal liability, compliance costs, and exposure to lawsuits from penalized employees. [S2] [S3]

drawbacks.text: The 24-hour verbal reporting clock starts the moment a company has actual knowledge of a serious danger, which in practice could force reports of preliminary or disputed findings before engineering or scientific review is complete, and the 'responsible corporate officer' definition could sweep in many managers who did not personally make the decision. [S3]
The mandate overlaps with existing agency reporting rules for product hazards, so it would add a parallel criminal enforcement path and compliance burden on top of current regulatory regimes. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real but one-sided in design: the public gain is faster warnings about products or practices that could kill or seriously injure people, plus protection for the workers who speak up. The costs are heavier compliance obligations and criminal exposure that could be triggered early in a company's internal review. The bill tries to limit abuse by requiring 'actual knowledge' of a danger 'not readily apparent to a reasonable person' and by preserving existing law, but the short deadline and broad officer definition would still create pressure to over-report. [S3]

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2014 and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 16, 2014 and, the same day, was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary. [S5] [S1]
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015. [S5] [S1]
The bill had a Democratic sponsor and two Democratic cosponsors and no recorded Republican support or opposition in its history. [S4] [S3]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that conceal serious product dangers are better off: they face no new criminal penalties for delaying warnings, and executives keep the practical shield of corporate-paid penalties and at-will retaliation against employees who speak up.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill establishing criminal penalties for failing to inform and warn of serious dangers. [S1] [S3]

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on July 16, 2014 and took no recorded action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress. [S5]

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; the record shows no votes, so no partisan split was ever measured. [S4] [S5]

industries.note: The bill would expose their executives to prison for sitting on knowledge of serious dangers and start a 24-hour reporting clock, directly limiting the practice of quietly managing hazards. That speed of warning is what protects consumers and workers. [S2] [S3]
Covered services are included alongside products, so companies whose practices endanger people would face the same reporting mandates and criminal penalties. [S3]

Individual officers with responsibility and authority over dangerous products or practices would face up to five years in prison, and companies could not pay their fines for them, ending the practice of firms absorbing the cost of individual punishment. [S3]
